title: The Properties of Water
short: Water is polar, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds. That gives cohesion, adhesion, surface tension, a high specific heat, its power as a solvent, and ice that floats.
trouble: Students think the bonds inside a water molecule break when water boils. Boiling breaks the hydrogen bonds between molecules; the molecules themselves stay H₂O.

blocks.html: Water is so common that it seems plain. It is not. Almost every special thing about water comes from the hydrogen bonds you met in The Elements and Bonds of Life.

Water is polar, so its molecules stick to each other by hydrogen bonds. That gives water cohesion, adhesion, surface tension, a high specific heat, a high heat of vaporization, great power as a solvent, and ice that floats.

head: Property
What hydrogen bonds do
Where life uses it
rows: Water molecules cling to each other
A water strider walks on a pond; a column of water holds together as it is pulled up a tree
Water clings to other polar surfaces
Water creeps up the narrow tubes (xylem) of a plant
Energy goes into breaking hydrogen bonds before molecules speed up
Lakes, oceans and bodies change temperature slowly
Escaping molecules carry a lot of energy away
δ+ and δ− ends surround ions and polar molecules
Sugars, salts and many proteins dissolve in blood and cytoplasm
In ice, hydrogen bonds lock molecules into an open lattice, about 9% larger in volume
Lakes freeze from the top down, and life survives under the ice

blocks.name: bi-molecule
blocks.cap: Each water molecule can hydrogen-bond to as many as four neighbors.

blocks.html: Specific heat is the energy needed to warm 1 gram by 1 °C. For water it is about 4.18 J (1 calorie); for dry sand it is about a fifth of that. When you heat water, much of the energy breaks hydrogen bonds instead of making molecules move faster, so the temperature rises slowly. The heat needed is $q = m \times c \times \Delta T$.

blocks.q: How much energy warms 200 g of water from 15 °C to 25 °C? (c = 4.18 J/(g·°C))

blocks.title: Match the property
blocks.q: Why does sweating cool you more than the same amount of a liquid that evaporates easily, like rubbing alcohol on a table?
steps: To evaporate, a water molecule must break all its hydrogen bonds.
That takes a lot of energy, which comes from your skin.
This is water's high heat of vaporization.

blocks.html: Thinking that boiling breaks water molecules apart into hydrogen and oxygen. Steam is still H₂O. Boiling breaks the weak hydrogen bonds between molecules so they can fly off as a gas; the strong covalent bonds inside each molecule stay whole. Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen gas takes a chemical reaction, such as passing electricity through it.
